utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. Good morning to you, sir. The affirmation you made at the beginning of your evidence still applies, of course. Mr. Borovic I think, may have some questions for you. Mr. Borovic. MR. BOROVIC [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I have no questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner, you are suddenly thrust into center stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: That's fine. Good morning. Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: My name is Philip Weiner. I am with the Office of the Prosecutor. I will be asking you some questions today. Okay?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, in your report, sir, you described the tasks of the security organ, based on the Rules and the doctrine that's on pages 11 through 13 of the new version. Just asking you if you could describe those rules.

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And, sir, you knew that Major Sljivancanin was performing duties outside of those tasks and responsibilities of a security organ.

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the basis of what I have been able to study, I had made a limited conclusion that there had been such activities, but I did not really study this in particular, because these activities fall outside of the scope of the security organ's activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: But you, sir, were aware, even though you didn't mention it in your report, that Major Sljivancanin was performing of other officers.

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not study those duties, but as I was studying the materials, I did come across such situations.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So, sir, were you aware that there's been testimony in this trial that Major Sljivancanin performed the duties of the assistant commander of logistics? Were you aware of that testimony? And that's at page 14433 to 34.

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, I was not aware of that. And I did not have such data at my disposal when I was drafting my report, so this is the first time I hear something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Were you aware, sir, that there was testimony also on that page that Major Sljivancanin was performing tasks or duties of the assistant commander for morale?

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, again, we have the same situation as the one that I outlined above.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. And so I assume you also were not aware that Major Sljivancanin -- or that there's been testimony that Major Sljivancanin was performing duties of the commander of the 1st Assault Detachment. And that's at page 14434 in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, right at the beginning, I said that I had taken cognisance of some of these activities. But these were not interesting to me at all, because they were not relevant for the work and the function of security organs. They did not interfere with the function of the security organ.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Well, sir, were you aware that there was testimony here that by getting involved or being involved in the logistical needs of the Vukovar TO that Major Sljivancanin was interfering with the responsibilities of the commander of the 1st Assault Detachment? Were you aware of that testimony, sir?

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I did not have any such data at my disposal. But even if I had them at my disposal, that would not affect my conclusions about his performance of his duties and tasks that belong within the purview of the security organ.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, were you also aware that Major Sljivancanin or Security Organ Sljivancanin was performing the duties of the chief of artillery? That's at page 14435. Were you aware of that, sir?

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I did not know that he had the duty of the chief of artillery, but I did find some information that he did participate in the correction of artillery fire. And this is something that bears taking into account.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Were you aware, sir, that Major Sljivancanin wanted to be the centre of attention, to be on television and in the newspaper frequently? Were you aware of that, sir?

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know about his media presence. And I did know about it, but it was not anything of interest to me because this was just part of his personality, of his public appearance. Most of my attention was devoted to the function and to researching and studying whether this in any way affected or led him to perhaps not comply or violate the rules of service and of performing his function.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, would you agree that press relations is not one of the regular duties of a security organ?

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those contacts are not within the purview in the strict sense, and this is why I did not pay any attention to them at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, were you aware that Major Sljivancanin was firing a 60-millimetre mortar for television, for the television networks? And that's on page 14434. Were you aware of that, sir?

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not know about that as you now put it to me, but I did hear that he had appeared in such situations where these activities had been taking place.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you agree, sir, that the firing of mortars is not a regular duty of a security organ.

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware of that. I listed the regular duties in my report and I still maintain that this is the fact and this is what must be the key issue for an expert studying the work of security organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You said you were aware that Major Sljivancanin was correcting artillery fire in October of -- or I'll add in October of 1991 is when that occurred. Would you agree that it's unusual for a security organ to be correcting artillery fire?

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a rule, it is unusual, but there are situations where there may be reasons to do something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Were you aware -- sir, do you know if Major Sljivancanin has any training in either the firing of mortars or the correcting of artillery fire? Colonel Panic testified that he didn't believe he had any.

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what training Colonel Sljivancanin underwent. I'm an air force man, and I don't know what kind of training infantry or artillery and other units of the ground forces receive. So I didn't even try to find out what kind of training they undergo and who has the obligation to actually undergo such training in the ground forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Are you aware that Major Sljivancanin demanded that General Zivota Panic be informed that he was correcting artillery fire and then it was mentioned in the war diary that he did so?

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I analysed the combat documents, and I did come across this entry. And as an expert, I can say a couple of things about this issue if you're interested in them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Well, first, sir, do you agree that the routine correction of artillery fire does not deserve mention in Operation Group South, in the Operation Group South war diary?

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depends on the actual case. As a rule, it is as you say, but there are exceptions where it is of extreme importance to record something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Would you agree, sir, that security organ training does not include the correction of artillery fire?

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not the training of the security organs. It is an activity that, in that specific case, may have been the result of a certain situation arising in the area where there was an artillery fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Are you aware, sir, that there's been testimony in this case that Major Sljivancanin was firing a mortar with the chief of artillery to investigate the quality of the gunpowder, to determine how humid or damp the gunpowder was? Were you aware of that? And that testimony is at page 14434-435.

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: If Major Sljivancanin did it to test the humidity of the gunpowder, then the question is whether he did it to determine whether the gunpowder was humid because of improper storage or for any other reason that may be of interest for a security organ.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, does security organ training including -- I'm sorry. Does the training of a security organ include the testing of gunpowder for mortars?

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: The training of the security organs does include the investigation of any phenomena that may threaten the security in the units, the equipment, weapons, and all the other assets used by the Yugoslav People's Army; hence, this necessity. If there is any defect in the weapons, the mortars, equipment, other types of materiel that may have been caused the deliberately, the security organs may determine whether there was this intention to damage the equipment and who is behind this.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, wouldn't you agree that the individuals who fire a mortar and the chief of artillery are in a much better position than Major Sljivancanin to analyse the quality of the gunpowder, the people who do it on a daily basis?

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this case, it could be said that Major Sljivancanin was not analysing the gunpowder, he was trying to determine the causes that may have led to the fact that the gunpowder was not in -- of appropriate quality.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, you're just speculating. Again, the question is: Wouldn't you agree that the individuals who fire a mortar and the chief of artillery are in a much better position than Major Sljivancanin to analyse the quality of the gunpowder? These are the people who fire the mortars on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will reply to your question because you apparently misunderstood the second part of my previous answer. As for the analysis of the quality, definitely, the people who are professionals are the most appropriate people to analyse it. But as to the causes that led to this situation, this is something that is outside of the purview of the artillery people.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, I'm asking about the firing of the mortar and the reviewing of the gunpowder -- evaluating the gunpowder. You agree that the people in artillery or the members of the infantry who fire the mortars, they are the people who are in the best position to review and analyse the firing and the gunpowder.

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is that a question?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes. It is, sir.

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. Fine. Yes. This is the crux of the matter. The first element is the cause, and cause has nothing to do with determining the quality.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, I'd appreciate if you just answer the question. You're trying to answer other questions. Just please answer the question that's asked. Now, sir, you drafted your report during the late summer --

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I make a comment, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I taught in the security training centre for eight years, and I was supposed to convey to my students in the training centre all the threats that the Yugoslav People's Army faced. Among the activities were diversions, sabotage activities, and other forms of internal threats that may affect the normal functioning of the armed forces. I did not go into the technical matters that may have resulted from those threats, and that is why I gave you this kind of answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that Mr. Weiner did not give an opportunity to the witness to reply, and his question was to defect -- in fact, he wanted to ask about why Mr. Sljivancanin participated in the correction of fire, but apparently he didn't want to hear the answer. But now the witness has, I think, given an explanation. So my objection is groundless now, but I still would like to point out that Mr. Weiner might let the witness answer the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I asked a specific question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Sorry, I was inviting you to carry on. I think enough has been said.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You know well that you moved to another question without allowing the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, you drafted this report in the late summer, I believe fall of this year.

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: The fall of this year.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And in drafting your report, you utilised and relied upon Colonel Panic's statement that he gave to the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: At start, I did it in the only way that was possible, and then there were some corrections that could be done within the limits of what was available.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: In drafting your report, you utilised or relied upon the statement that Colonel Panic gave to the Office of the Prosecutor; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And when you filed your report, you had a number of references to the statement of Colonel Panic.

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And in fact, on page 2 in the introduction, you refer to the sources, including documents and statements made by some persons in de jure form and during the stand as witnesses.

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me have a look.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: The second paragraph in the introduction.

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't find it. Can you give me a more specific reference, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: It's the second paragraph of the introduction: "During the work on this report, I have made reference to certain sources, i.e., documents and statements made by some persons in de jure form or during their stand as a witness."

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner, yes, I did find the relevant portion. Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And in the statements that you're referring to, you're referring to the statement of Colonel Panic.

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, just as a quick question: Did you ever speak with Colonel Panic concerning his statement or his testimony or in relation to the issues in this case?

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: I met Colonel Panic at the special court in Belgrade during the Ovcara trial which I attended, and we actually met there for the first time. I had not met him before, and I also met him at some point later on when the question was whether he would testify or not at this trial because of his family situation. And we had a very perfunctory conversation about all those issues. This was not a situation to study or to discuss this in any detail. But when I saw his statement, I thought it would be good to check some issues from the security point of view. But because he had just been the Chief of Staff on the not performed any command functions, I thought this could be done without that. My contact with him on those two occasions was of a very perfunctory occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, last Friday, counsel had indicated that you had spoken with Mr. Sljivancanin. Have you spoken with any other witnesses of this case?

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: The question about discussing a case has two aspects. The first aspect is using the normal, usual terminology; and the other aspect is me acting as an expert witness. There were contacts, but not with me in my capacity as an expert. There were many conversations. I had spent quite a chunk of my life working in the army. I know a lot of people. I'm in touch with a lot of people, but some of these contacts were simply not official or anything to do with the business in hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Which witnesses have you spoken with?

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first type of encounter or conversation was sometimes a matter of coincidence, meeting people I didn't personally know but who I knew to be in a certain place. For example, Ljubisa Vukasinovic whom I had not known before. I would go on business to the security administration and sometimes find him there and just chat with him. This one was specifically a rather accidental meeting, and I knew nothing about that person really.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So any other witnesses other than the accused, Sljivancanin, Ljubisa Vukasinovic, or Colonel Panic?

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm trying to remember all the faces filing past me in these conversations. Even some of the people I didn't know well, I didn't know would be appearing as witnesses one day when I met them. I might go wrong. It's difficult to remember them all, but I think there was this once by pure coincidence. By pure accident I met Susic, but I would hardly have known him from Adam, that I would know that he would be called as a witness. It was then that I knew who the person was, but I certainly never discussed this sort of business with him at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, on Monday, certain sources of your report were changed. You didn't change your facts or conclusions, but you changed the sources to reflect not their statements but the -- basically, not the statements of Panic, but the trial testimony of Panic; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: I tried to check which of the facts might affect my conclusions in an essential way or change anything about my conclusions. Maybe there were bits of phrasing there that would now look differently, but the gist of the conclusions would not change. Therefore, it was possible to cross-reference these to evidence given before this Trial Chamber, as well as to material that I had used previously. I don't think it would have changed the gist of my conclusions, and that's why they remain as they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, have you read the transcripts in this case or have you followed this case, all the witnesses in this case over the Internet?

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I haven't read the transcripts off the Internet. I just familiarised myself with the original evidence given in this case. The situation being what it was, it was necessary to identify only those portions of evidence that might affect my expert report. I didn't go into command. I didn't go into logistics, that sort of thing. I didn't know that much about any other activities. I did know about security to the extent that an expert would be expected to know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, would you agree that when you drafted your report and you relied on Colonel Panic's statement, and later his testimony, you were selective in the information that you included. In your own words, you looked just to the parts relating to the security organ.

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, I was selective. It's my job to be selective. As a security officer, I am required to identify facts that have to do with security. I must be able to focus on those. I must be able to study and analyse them. And this requires a selective approach.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And would you agree, sir, that if the facts conflicted with your conclusions or were not helpful to Mr. Sljivancanin, you ignored certain facts and information?

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner, could you please quote these facts? That would probably help me to see why I understood them or omitted them. It could be either of these, it's just that I would be hard put to say now. I have nothing based on which to conclude that I did anything like that. I have no reason to admit anything to do with security that might shed any light on particular functions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Well, sir, you agreed than relied on Colonel Panic's report when you drafted your statement. And if we look at Colonel Panic's report, you should have a notebook in front of you. And we have a copy of his OTP statement in Serbian, or I have a copy right here for you if you like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I might be jumping the gun in expectation of the remaining part of the question, but I think this line of questioning is contrary to your own decision, Your Honours, the one that was made when Mr. Forca was in this courtroom and when Mr. Weiner wanted to confront him with the evidence of Mr. Miroljub Vujovic at the Belgrade trial. That was in relation to Captain Radic's command. The page reference is 13358 and 13359. You, Your Honour, said at the time that this was not an appropriate approach. I was wondering if Mr. Weiner was now heading much the same way as before perhaps. So that's what my reaction is about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: May I say briefly, Mr. Lukic, that if Mr. Weiner is heading that way, this situation is different, because we are dealing with an expert witness as expressly said that for forming his opinion, he has relied on what other people have said. And Mr. Weiner is now asking him to identify what passages he has relied on and is pointing out other passages that he has not, as I understand what Mr. Weiner is trying to do. If it is the case that there has been selectivity which has an effect of favouring or not favouring your client, then that will affect the weight we can give to the opinion formed. So it's because it's an expert witness who has expressly relied on certain material that Mr. Weiner is entitled to explore that material with him. Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you. We have copies for the Court and for all counsel and translators. Tab 26, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: You can use tab 26 or you have a copy there, separate copy of the statement, sir.

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have a copy in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, I invite your attention to paragraph 48 which is on page 12 in the English and B/C/S. For the ERN or the e-court, it's 0461-8179 to 0461-8208 and it's page 8190. Now, sir, you previously indicated, earlier in your testimony, that you didn't have certain information available to you about Mr. Sljivancanin acting outside of his duties. Could we look at paragraph 48 where it says: "Even though all responsibilities within the staff of the Guards Motorised Brigade (or OG South) were clearly defined, Sljivancanin went well beyond what was required of him by his job description. Major Veselin Sljivancanin talked a lot at the daily briefings of the OG South command in Negoslavci. He did not limit his activities to what was usually expected of a head of security service. "Instead, he also discussed the situation on the battlefield, mentioning what he saw and making suggestions as to what should be done. Sljivancanin also spoke about the logistical needs (food, ammunition, other) of local Serbian TO units at the briefings, even though we had an officer who was responsible for that, the assistant commander for logistics. All these things exceeded Sljivancanin's professional duties as head of the security service." The next paragraph he continues: "Sljivancanin also did things that he was not supposed to do. This would sometimes elicit criticism from the commander of the Guards Motorised Brigade, Colonel Mile Mrksic. Once Sljivancanin went on his own initiative to an infantry unit in order to fire a 60 millimetre mortar. This was even shown on TV. I have been shown the war diary of the Guards Motorised Brigade ERN B/C/S 0293-5434-0293-5482. ERN English L010-0496-L010-0537; entry of 13th October 1991 which says Sljivancanin demanded that General Zivota Panic be informed of the fact that he had personally corrected artillery fire in the Mitnica section. "It is unusual for a security officer to correct artillery fire; there are other officers responsible for that. Otherwise, correction of artillery fire is a routine task in military operations, and does not deserve mention in the war diary." Did you mention either of those paragraphs in your report indicating that Security Organ Sljivancanin was performing acts outside of his duties and responsibilities?

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I never said I had no information like that. What I did say is that I knew about some of the activities carried out by Sljivancanin, and I viewed them in the light of his function as a security officer. I wanted to know about any possible interferences of these activities with his remit as a security officer. That's what I meant when I said before that I was trying to do a selective reading. Secondly, when we discuss artillery fire, Panic is not a security officer, and he does not have a professional outlook on this. And this is the last time I'm going to say that. Secondly, Panic described the activities taken by Sljivancanin outside his security role. The commander knew, Panic knew, the other officers knew, but this is not a security function and it's not the subject of my investigation. I'm not looking at Veselin Sljivancanin as an officer in the Guards Brigade, I'm assessing his role as a security officer. That's the question I'm dealing with. I can say the same thing that Panic did but that has absolutely no bearing on my expert report.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, when you mentioned what duties Major Sljivancanin performed according to the rules, regulations, and doctrine, would you agree that you omitted describing his acts that were outside of the duties of the security organ?

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I omitted that. That is not part of his remit as a security officer. That remains to be proven what else he did. I was trying to analyse what he was supposed to do. Now, what he actually did, I don't know. It's for those who were actually there to find. My task was to shed light on his actual function and to ago tan whether that was in keeping with all the regulations that applied.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, your answer was: "I was trying to analyse what he was supposed to do. Now what he actually did, I don't know. It's for others who were actually there to find." Your report concerns doctrine and what a person should do according to doctrine. You were not present to witness any of his actions that he took in Vukovar; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wasn't present. I'm an expert who wasn't present. The information was available to me regardless of who was where. Your Honours, may I be allowed a comment at this point?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Reading this now, I did say that I was clearly familiar with this these facts. I'm a security expert. I consider that anything that the command had to do about Sljivancanin is certainly nothing for a security expert to worry about. A security expert answers the following question: What was Sljivancanin supposed to do? And not the question about what Sljivancanin was not supposed to do. And that was my principal guideline in writing my report. My report would have ended up being a very different report had my original role been a very different one to begin with, but it didn't happen to be. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Let's move to another area. In your report on page 48, the section begins with footnote 80, the evacuation of the hospital in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: Give me a minute to find that, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right. Yes, sir. Please, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, initially in that page you attempt to describe the roles and assignment of Major Sljivancanin during the evacuation of the hospital, and then you write on pages -- it's now 50 and 51, the last -- it's the last sentence in the English on page 50, it's paragraph 1.5. Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: "Had Colonel Mrksic still decided contrary to the provisions of said regulations to assign the duties and to delegate a portion of his powers to Major Sljivancanin thus empowering him to command the evacuation operation, he ought to have given him an order in writing." Then below that in paragraph 1.11, you conclude that without any writing, it's your conclusion that he did not command the evacuation; or that without any writing, you were not able to conclude that he commanded the evacuation. Correct?

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is a little bit of confusion there, but we'll try to shed some light on this. There are certain positions here that are important for our general understanding or, rather, for you to know why I wrote it like this. Firstly, we discussed, yesterday, who had the power to give orders to any security officer in their own units, or, rather, what the rules specifically envisage in their item -- or Article 48. The rules for the work of security organs, which tasks they can be given. Their purview rules out the possibility of their involvement outside of their strictest remit, even at the urging of the Federal Secretary for National Defence himself. So that's as concerns the first portion of this question. The next thing is the possibility of deviations and what form that might take. If, indeed, there are reasons, which in this specific case I fail to recognise for any deviations from the rules that applied, the reasons have to be provided, as well as specific tasks for whoever is supposed to act outside the regulations, since consequences can potentially be serious and the responsibility rests with whoever makes such a request. Another thing is any person involved in anything outside their remit must speak up and say whether they feel capable of carrying out that sort of task at all. And there must be a stand-in while this person is away, because the situation faced by security organs is a very peculiar one indeed. Their powers are personal powers. They have IDs. Once they are temporarily or permanently removed from their establishment duties, they no longer have the same powers, and they cannot exercise those powers. They can only exercise those powers for as long as they remain in the function to which they are appointed within a unit. In one word, there are serious impediments to this remaining the way that it was. What it takes is for the whole thing to be regulated through a set of rules and regulations in order to avoid further serious potential serious infractions and violations. That's why my statement was put in a relatively mild form. I said it takes further investigation to see what the reasons might have been for what eventually happened. I'm not saying this should by no means have been done. All I'm saying is there should be a certain explanation to show why this course of action was taken. I thank you for your patience.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So you're saying that Colonel Mrksic could have appointed Major Sljivancanin to command the evacuation as long as it was done in writing?

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not what I'm saying. I'm saying if there is to be a deviation from the rules, or something done in contravention of the rules, there is a procedure that is applied. At least as long as he was in keeping with this particular set of rules, there was no way he could have allowed himself to deviate. So that's what I was saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, that's according to the rules and doctrine. But you know that while drafting your report, you had information in your possession that Colonel Mrksic had assigned Major Sljivancanin to command the evacuation operation; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not correct, and I'm going to tell you why. I have no document unambiguously indicating that. You're asking me a question. Please allow me to answer the question, and then you're perfectly free to ask m additional questions if you deem that necessary. I am painfully aware of the fact that time is short, but that doesn't mean that I can't answer my questions. The first thing is that in the situation that --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner, allow the witness to continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: That's continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. You see, the situation that we are discussing now, any situation is a doctrine. I, as an expert, can't stretch the doctrine too far or consider any situations that are actually use the doctrine. My task was to place this inside the context of an doctrine and then exam it. It was in this sense that I was looking for a fact that would unambiguously ambiguously confirm that Sljivancanin had received an order like that with those very conditions, because that's what the doctrine requires. I didn't find that, so I couldn't actually establish that in my actual opinion. That's actually a natural consequence, isn't it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, let's get away from doctrine and look at facts. You indicated that you looked at the testimony of Colonel Panic, and you're aware or are you aware that Colonel Panic affirmed in his testimony that on November 19th, that he was present when Colonel Mrksic announced that Major Sljivancanin would be in command of the evacuation at Vukovar Hospital? That's at pages 14382 to 14383. Are you aware of that testimony, sir?

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: If what you just asked me was perfectly clear, then this position here would merely be unnecessary. Since this entire thing exceeds the framework of doctrine, I had to look at facts to see what had caused it. I found nothing. I don't have an answer to that question. I did see that position. I saw Colonel Panic's statement. I could say that Colonel Panic is right, but the doctrine says that he is not right, that Mrksic wasn't right. If they were right, I have to find what the cause is, what their original position is. I'm an expert witness. I'm not a witness who was briefed. Thank you for asking me all these questions, but regrettably, I do believe that this is the only answer I can provide. It just happens to be that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I may be butting in again. But it seems to me that this page that I'm reading, he was confronted with a part of the statement and that this is not contained in the witness testimony, but perhaps we should leave that for redirect. Mr. Weiner said testimony and not statement, and what was quoted was a part of the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would be happy to read it and confront him with that if that would make Mr. Lukic happy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That may be very interesting to you and to Mr. Lukic. But if you listen to the witness, it's not very interesting to him. He's told you what he saw as the relevance of this and the way he perceived it. So while you two may want to argue about that in final address to us, it's not going to help us learn more about the witness's opinions and the basis for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, you never stated in your report that Colonel Mrksic tasked Major Sljivancanin to be in command of the evacuation operation. You never stated that, did you?

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't state that, and the reasons we already have before us.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you never stated that Colonel Panic was present or witnessed Mrksic when he announced Sljivancanin was in command of the evacuation operation.

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we all had been listening carefully to this discussion, we would have come to the conclusion that I had already answered this question. Mr. Weiner, I do have to apologise, but I want to save some time for both of us. If you have any further questions, perhaps we can move on, because I have already given answers to these questions repeatedly. And in the end, the impression might be that I have not given proper answers at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, yesterday, you were told in regard to Panic's testimony in relation to attending a meeting that the Mrksic Defence had challenged the credibility of that testimony. And you said at page 55: "If a witness who was actually there says that a decision was accepted, I have no other interpretation to offer apart from what that can be taken to mean at face value; namely, that is decision was accepted." Sir, that's what you said in relation to a question yesterday when you were asked about some testimony. There was a decision that Panic has mentioned in his statement and in his testimony. Unlike yesterday's testimony, you're not accepting it or mentioning it in your report.

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: This state of fact that we're talking about falls outside the scope of the doctrine, but we are now discussing doctrine, in fact. What we are talking about now is if a decision was made, whether this decision was proper or improper in accordance with the doctrine. I don't want to go into whether this decision had actually been made. I did not find enough evidence of the proper kind that would make me claim that. But if this decision was indeed made, it is up to the Trial Chamber to find whether the decision was made or not and whether it was valid or not. As far as I, as an expert, am concerned, my actions were quite proper. I studied all the events, imprecise as they were, and I put them in the context of an expert report which has strictly defined limits. Everything else is the issue of finding the truth, and it is not up to me to decide what is truth and what is not, which statements were true and which were not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, in your report, you describe doctrine and you indicated that you didn't believe the appointment could be made according to doctrine. But you did not place in a footnote or note in that report: However, there is testimony, there is a statement, there is a witness that Sljivancanin was named the commander or ordered to be the commander of the hospital evacuation. You didn't state that, did you?

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not put it in my report because doctrine does not give us answers to that, and I was not there as an eye witness to say whether Sljivancanin was appointed or not. And this was not put quite in those terms. There is still some uncertainty there. I didn't understand it that way, but this does not deny or confirm what I claimed. So I am not claiming that he was not. I'm just saying this is how things are, if he was and these -- this is how things are if he wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, could you look back at Colonel Panic's statement, paragraph 72, please, which you relied upon when you drafted your report back in the late summer or early fall. It's on page 18 in the English and B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please give me the paragraph reference, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: 72, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before the question, I would just like Mr. Vuga to speak slowly, because we have problems with the transcript because the interpretation is rather complex.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm sure the witness heard that, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I will read the paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: "It is unusual for a security officer to be given responsibility for an evacuation operation. However, I assume Mrksic appointed Sljivancanin to the position because of the important role the security organ had to play in the operation. Sljivancanin was not only responsible for the selection of prisoners, he commanded the entire evacuation of people to Sremska Mitrovica. This implied that Sljivancanin was able to issue orders to the military police or any other unit in the operation." Did I read that correctly, sir?

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weiner, you read it correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, 12 hours prior to the evacuation, Colonel Mrksic places Sljivancanin in charge or he -- according to this, "he commanded the entire evacuation of people to Sremska Mitrovica." You didn't mention this anywhere in your report, isn't that correct, not even in a footnote?

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I explained that, but let me go back to what I said initially. I asked you to check whether we have indeed resolved this. So now I have to, again, ask the question. If -- it is not usual, but I assume in a situation like this I face a dilemma. What must be assumed here in relation to the authority and other issues that are outside of the doctrine. And I shouldn't speculate in this manner and rely on that. As far as the footnote is concerned, that would not change anything, in my view. So this wasn't important for me. This is why I formed this kind of expert opinion. There was no other reason for me to leave this out, apart from the fact that from the point of view of my expert report, it did not either support the view that this would be in accordance with the doctrine or support the belief that this was outside of the doctrine that the procedure that was not in accordance with the doctrine was complied with.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, you've indicated in your report that there was very few documents concerning the evacuation; and also yesterday, you said that there were no documents indicating who Mrksic placed in charge of the evacuation. Wouldn't you agree that when you were drafting your report, the best evidence you had available as to who was in charge of the evacuation was that Panic statement where he says Mrksic assigned Major Sljivancanin to command the evacuation?

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner, a word has been left out which is very important from this text, and this word is I could not unequivocally determine that Major Sljivancanin -- so there is still this dilemma that Major Sljivancanin was assigned to command the evacuation. So it is very important to read every word here, because the word "unequivocally" put me in a position where I could still consider whether this was so or not, in the belief that this would be resolved at trial. Everything else was clear or clarified. So this is simply the nature of this issue. We are -- we do not differ here, but we do differ in the sense of the interpretation of the texts. When you leave out a word when you interpret the text, then this poses some problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, you had no problem following Colonel Panic's testimony in relation to the government meeting at Velepromet and accepting that, even though it's contested. But here, you will not follow -- on that same basis, you will not follow and abide by Colonel Panic's testimony; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: The situation is quite different from this issue that we now are trying to resolve. First of all, Panic was at the government session in a different role in relation to the role he played at the briefing he attended at the government session, Panic. I assume this was not usual. And he did not state his views on any facts that were presented there that were of interest for me in my assessment. This was something that I used to orient myself and to -- I drew my conclusions based on that. So what we have here are two completely different positions and two completely different situations. It's not a matter of applying different principles, it's just that these two situations are completely different from the point of view of an expert, in particular, a security expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: But sir, even as a security expert, and writing a report or drafting a report, you had an obligation to state what the doctrine was but indicate, be it in the text or in a footnote, indicate that there is evidence, however, or there is testimony, however, or there is a statement, however, indicating that Colonel Mrksic did, in fact, order Major Sljivancanin to be in charge of the evacuation, out of fairness.

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: I gave you the reasons that led me to conclude that this was not done, and here we have this footnote; and even with that footnote, nothing would change in terms of the expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Well let's continue, sir. You mention that there was a group of officers from the security administration including Colonel Vujic that were sent to OG South; do you recall that or are you aware of that, sir?

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And are you aware that Colonel Vujic met with Major Sljivancanin in the early morning hours of November 20th around 1.00 or 2.00 a.m.; are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm trying to remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So around 1.00 or 2.00 a.m., we're dealing with, approximately, five hours before the evacuation. Are you aware that Sljivancanin told Vujic, and I'm reading on page 4530 at lines 18 to 20: "Major Sljivancanin said that the hospital was to be vacated according to an evacuation plan, that he would personally be in charge of this mission." Were you aware of that testimony, sir?

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to say that I missed that statement completely; and if I had had that statement, I would have been able to tell you what my view of it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So, sir, in your conclusion, and you can tell your view about it, but I just want to ask you this first. You didn't -- or in your opinion or report, you haven't indicated that 12 hours before the evacuation, there's testimony that Sljivancanin was placed in charge of the evacuation, and that five hours before the evacuation, Colonel -- I'm sorry, Major Sljivancanin tells Colonel Vujic that he was in charge. You now have two statements: One from the accused and one witnessing Colonel Mrksic performing the act of ordering Sljivancanin to be in charge. Did you take either of those statements into account as part of your conclusion?

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: I presented my view of the first one, because I had it in front of me. And I cannot anything about the second one, because I didn't see it. I cannot give you any views or any explanations on an item that I have never seen.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that Mr. Weiner perhaps did express himself properly in English. But the interpretation into B/C/S, I'm referring to page 29, line 15, it says here that you had two statements, one of the accused and the other one who testified what Mrksic had said. And in fact, Mr. Mrksic -- Mr. Weiner was now talking about Mr. Vujic's statement. So the question was to the facts that Mr. Vujic testified to in his evidence or statement not Mr. Sljivancanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: All right. I'll try and clarify that. Approximately, five hours before the evacuation, there is testimony that Major Sljivancanin told Colonel Vujic that he was in charge of the evacuation plan. First, are you aware of that testimony?

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: The same reply as before: No, I'm not aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'd ask you to assume the truth of that statement, sir, that Sljivancanin says that he is in charge of the evacuation. Does that assist you in determining who was in charge -- who was in charge of the evacuation on November 20th, 1991?

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: We now have to go back to the very beginning in order to get a full picture of the situation. I was not able to talk about the position that was taken with regard to the facts that I had in the first version. That relates to Lieutenant-Colonel Panic. Now we have a situation that should give birth to a new hypothesis, and I really have to get some additional data and to analyse it to see what all this entails. I cannot give you any conclusions on the basis of those assumptions as to who was actually in charge of the. I cannot do that, and we should really perhaps leave it to the Trial Chamber to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Well, just one more question, sir. Would you agree that Sljivancanin's statement, at 1.00 to 2.00 in the morning, that he was in charge of the evacuation is corroborative or consistent with Colonel Panic's testimony that he was present when Mrksic placed Sljivancanin in charge of the evacuation?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, whether I, as an expert, can agree with your suggestion, I can't tell whether something is important or not. I simply can say that anyone who was not an expert, if he heard such a statement, he would agree. But as an expert, I can only answer as an expert. I cannot fit it into my doctrine or the information that had I put under the question mark; and, therefore, I cannot make this conclusion that would, in fact, be a hypothesis because I'm an expert. If you ask me to do that as a non-expert, then yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, is it time for a break now, or would you like me to continue with a new subject?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That's a gentle hint, Mr. Weiner. It's four minutes early but we will break now. We resume at ten minutes to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. Let us continue. Yesterday, you testified that the barracks were the most -- or could be the safest and most secure place in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is right, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, just for a matter of record, you didn't perform any security evaluation of the Vukovar barracks in November 1991. You personally didn't do so.

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Were you in the Vukovar barracks or in Vukovar itself in November of 1991?

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Basically, you have no firsthand knowledge as to the security of the Vukovar barracks. You're basing your testimony on doctrine, rules, regulations; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Are you aware that a Defence witness has, in fact, testified as to the level of security at the barracks in November 1991?

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm trying to think back to see what the information was that was available to me, and I realise there is something I failed to draw my about the security back in the barracks. But you would need to be more specific about the time period, the time period that you have in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Are you aware that a witness who was the chief of staff of the 80th Motorised Brigade, Mr. Danilovic, testified that he was part of a theme that analysed the condition of the barracks, so that the 80th Motorised Brigade could transfer its headquarters to that location. Are you aware of that testimony?

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Well let me read this to you and see if this refreshes your recollection. This is at page 12390 beginning on line 2. "When the town of Vukovar fell, there wasn't even the most basic conditions, security conditions or others prevailed at the barracks of Vukovar. You in this Court are familiar that we were the fact on the 22nd or 23rd requested for the barracks to be repaired, to be put into use because not even minimum conditions prevailed there. Ovcara was suitable for passing at least one night there so that the following day in daylight, the captured members of the ZNG and MUP of Croatian can or could be transferred. So the barracks, from our point of view, was completely unsatisfactory to accept POWs." Are you familiar with that testimony?

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not, but I must ask you one thing. Shall we discuss this. Is Ovcara and Vukovar the same thing in this particular reference, or are we only talking about Vukovar as a town?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: No. What the witness did is he discussed both. As he was discussing the safety of both and during his answer, which I read to you, he also threw in a section that Vukovar wasn't safe either. But are you familiar with his testimony that the barracks were not a safe place?

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll answer this question once we've explained whether Ovcara was part of Vukovar or whether the barracks was part of Vukovar unlike Ovcara which is actually outside Vukovar. If we can please get that clarified before we start doing anything else. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Again, sir, they are two separate locations. The witness indicated that both places were unsafe. So are you familiar with that testimony?

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner, nothing was safe in Vukovar at the time. That's what the combat documents suggest, not the barracks, not any other sector of Vukovar. Safety was the challenge in a different way once the operations had ceased but in a different way. I agree, no place in Vukovar was safe, but the question is which of all the unsafe places would be the safest place inside Vukovar itself. That is the subject of my report. I did not consider Ovcara as a facility or an installation from the security point of view, not the same way that I considered the barracks. I did not even compare the two. The only installation that I considered was the Vukovar barracks, regardless of how it was actually built, regardless of the fence around it. What I had in mind was the barracks as a military installation and everything that that normally implies. That's what I analysed under the circumstances that prevailed in Vukovar at the time and not disregarding those circumstances. So my conclusion was that in the whole of Vukovar from the point of view of security, despite all the threats, the barracks were still the safest place in Vukovar, if you take into account the standards normally applied in normal conditions. But even if these conditions are not met 100 percent, the barracks would still meet the requirements envisaged in all the rules and regulations as applying to any barracks. You might say that is the conclusion that I reached.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So, basically, your determination as to the barracks is based on the rules and regulations, but you were not there to confirm whether or not those rules and regulations were even followed?

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in your report, you mention Colonel Pavkovic. Would you agree, sir, that there is no evidence in this case linking Colonel Pavkovic to the selection or triage process at the Vukovar Hospital on November 20th?

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: We must disregard the briefing that preceded the hospital evacuation in which Colonel Pavkovic said what the criteria would be and who would be evacuated. There are certain points of contact, so to speak, when taking about Colonel Pavkovic. The EU monitors were present, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, we're talking about the selection process at 7.00 in the morning at the hospital when the EU monitors and the Red Cross were prevented from entering the area. So would you agree, sir, that there is no testimony indicating that Colonel Pavkovic was involved at that selection process, triage process at Vukovar Hospital on November 20th at 7.00 in the morning?

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now that's a more accurate question, and I do agree with this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And would you also agree that he was not involved in escorting those prisoners from the hospital to the barracks in that first group that -- the prisoners that left sometime around 9.00 or 10.00, who went from the hospital to the barracks?

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And would you also agree, sir, that Colonel Pavkovic was not involved in the decision to send the prisoners to the barracks on November 20th?

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found nothing to indicate that he was involved. Therefore, you could say that what you are putting to me is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Would you also agree that Colonel Pavkovic did not meet with the offices of the security administration and give them tasks to perform as part of the evacuation?

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Pavkovic didn't have any power over that group in any way.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, you would agree that he did not meet with them, those officers, and task them?

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether he met them or not. As for tasking them, I told you what I believe about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Would you agree that Colonel Pavkovic was not involved in the prisoner evacuation that occurred in the early morning of November 20th, that first group of prisoners that went from the hospital to the barracks?

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think we confirmed that in relation to the first part of your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And, sir, there has been testimony that Colonel Mrksic assigned Major Sljivancanin to command the evacuation. Would you agree that there has been no testimony in this case that anyone witnessed Colonel Mrksic assigning Colonel Pavkovic to command the evacuation?

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not consider that in terms of a task being given to Colonel Pavkovic, nor is there anything like that in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: But you would agree that there is no testimony that Colonel Mrksic assigned or that anyone witnessed Colonel Mrksic assigning Colonel Pavkovic to command the evacuation. You would agree with that, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found nothing to indicate otherwise. I did not look at that relationship at all. It was outside of the scope of what I was to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Finally, sir, there has been testimony that Major Sljivancanin stated that he was in charge of the mission to evacuate the hospital. Would you agree that there was no testimony in this trial where Colonel Pavkovic claimed to be in charge of the evacuation?

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the outset and in my report, I clearly stated that I had reached no unambiguous conclusion that it had been Sljivancanin, but I found no alternative either. So I didn't state any alternatives. So it must be the way you put it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, we've been talking about Colonel Pavkovic. Let's move to Major Sljivancanin for a short while. Now, you mentioned -- let's take it differently. There has been testimony of several actions taken by Major Sljivancanin that were not mentioned in your report. Were you aware that Major Sljivancanin tasks the commander of the 2nd Battalion of military police to bring Marin Vidic to the command at Negoslavci, and that the commander of the military police followed that command and did it?

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: The question of orders should be considered in a number of ways, or the question of command. I can't consider this, because I had no information to indicate that this was a command. So that's the problem I have answering this. I never found anything to suggest that this would have been a command. I'm saying this because a military police task in the security function is different from commanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: He tasked him to bring Marin Vidic, and Marin Vidic followed that task and did it. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that Marin Vidic was brought in for an interview. I don't know how that was done, nor did I analyse that in order to reach a conclusion as to who had ordered it. I didn't understand it to have been that way. But if indeed that's how it was, there must be evidence to that effect. I can hardly be expected to deny it. How could I possibly deny it. My analysis was not about how I came there but, rather, why he came there. So that's it, but I have no reason to deny anything either way.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. Are you aware that it was Major Sljivancanin who discussed the evacuation and hospital issues with the hospital director Mrs. Bosanac?

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Are you aware that it was Major Sljivancanin and Colonel Vujic who agreed or decided that the prisoners should be taken to the barracks? That's at page 13620.

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't their place to agree. The thing was one had to decide how the question of the patients and the wounded would be dealt with. They had to decide on a place, and then they agreed on the place having made an assessment on what the safest place would be. So that's a matter of assessment or agreement, if you like. But if they agreed, then their assessment must have been consistent. Vujic was a colonel and he was certainly more qualified to make assessments than Major Sljivancanin. He could have provided useful guidance for Sljivancanin on what to do and what the best course of action would be.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: But were you aware of that, sir, that Major Vujic and -- Colonel Vujic and Major Sljivancanin agreed upon the barracks?

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Weiner, I was not aware of that. I am speaking as an expert who can interpret the modus operandi applied in such situations like these.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Were you aware, sir, that there is testimony that it was Major Sljivancanin who held a meeting with the doctors at the Vukovar Hospital in the early morning of November 20th, 1991?

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was aware of that and that was consistent with what he was supposed to do in terms of security at the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Were you aware that it was Major Sljivancanin and the security organs who were responsible for the selection/triage process?

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: Major Sljivancanin was simply required be involved in the triage based on his powers and based on the tasks received from the superior command.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So you were aware that Major Sljivancanin and the security organs were responsible for the selection/triage process?

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what the report claims.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Were you aware that it was Major Sljivancanin who contacted General Vasiljevic concerning what to do with certain doctors who were believed to have committed war crimes?

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had nothing about that, no information.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Were you aware that it was Major Sljivancanin who ordered that certain persons be taken back from the barracks and returned to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And were you aware that Colonel Pavkovic told Sljivancanin to remove the journalists from the Vukovar visit. Major Sljivancanin declined and told the press to "feel free to record everything." That's at page 13642. Were you aware of that, sir?

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was aware of that, basically, but I didn't study that particular piece of information as anything that might be relevant for the security situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So these actions taken by Major Sljivancanin, if you didn't believe them to be relevant to the security situation, you didn't mention them at all in your report.

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't be expected to cover that much ground and mention everything that happened anywhere around Sljivancanin and include all of that in my report, because that would obscure the function itself. I had to pare back, as it were. I did that in each case where I decided that a limit had to be drawn, a distinction between the work done by a security officer and all the other functions that are sometimes contiguous. There is a complex reality of many competing functions all over a very short period of time and over a very small area. I had to isolate security facts, security-related issues that were material for my conclusions. The detail that you addressed did not contribute too much to me succeeding in painting the overall picture within the framework of my report. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you were discussing the security functions or you were focussing on the security functions according to doctrine; isn't that correct? Doctrine, rules, regulations?

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. That's certainly the case. My principal criterion, as I said at the outset, and in the course of my testimony yesterday, is to consistently and properly study the purview of the security organ, and also to use this as a criterion for assessing the subject of my report. And that brings us here. I dealt with security-related facts. I dealt with their potential meaning in the light of the doctrine. No doctrine, no potential meaning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Let's move on to another issue which you discussed in your report on page 66, paragraph 18. There's the first -- there's two paragraph 18s. The first one deals with why you believe the government would abide by the request, its request to try people from the hospital. It's between footnotes 140 and 141 in the text as found in the text between footnotes 140 and 141. You state four reasons, sir, do you see those? Why you believe that the government would, in fact, try those persons, those prisoners who were later murdered?

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: There are no footnotes or sources listed for any of those reasons, four reasons; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And those are your personal opinions as to why you think the government would act properly; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is my opinion as an expert in security matters who was the assistant commander for security -- assistant chief of security in the cabinet of the Federal Secretary of National Defence covering the entire territory of the SFRY; and as such, I was cognizant of some of the things that were happening in the political sphere. And I was also politically active as a member of the League of Communists, and I had personal knowledge about possible solutions for certain areas. My activities that followed testify to that. So on the basis of what I learned in this capacity, I believe that these elements could be the way they are presented in my report and that they could develop in those directions. That is why I put them in there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Well, let's talk about this so-called SAO government. You are aware that the testimony in this case is that that the government, the so-called SAO government, came from outside Vukovar? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand your question, Mr. Weiner. I didn't understand it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: No problem. Are you aware that the SAO government came from outside of Vukovar? This wasn't a government that was in Vukovar. They came from elsewhere, from the city of Dalj, D-a-l-j?

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware of the location itself or familiar with it, but it was outside of Vukovar, that much is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And are you aware that there was no civilian police unit in Vukovar in November of 1991?

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stated that in my report, and I confirm that now that I was aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And are you also aware that there were no judicial bodies in Vukovar in November of 1991?

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, since the normal governance was disrupted, definitely this was something that had to be done at a later stage. But at the time that we are talking about, it did not exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And are you aware that this SAO SBWS government was nowhere to be found prior to their appearance on November 20th in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not aware of that because I did not analyse the events that preceded this period that much. I found that this government, such as it was, functioned as it did in the prevailing circumstances. And that is why it is mentioned here like that and in no other way. And the course of the session and the information regarding that course indicated that there were the intentions -- there was the intention to follow this route as indicated here. So these two elements dove-tailed the trial and the other element that I mentioned here, and this is why I actually put it in here.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you're also aware that there were no orders to OG South to recognise that government?

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: The recognition of the government does not depend on OG South. It is not a political factor; it's an army. It's a military unit. The command of the 1st Military District could do something to recognise the government, because it was in the position to discuss and consider this issue as indicated by the document dated the 20th of November sent by the command of the 1st Military District regarding the establishment of the government to all the units active in this area. In this document, it actually defines the government in a manner that could serve as some kind of a guidance to its subordinates.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: But, sir, you don't know whether that document was sent to OG South, and you also know that OG South was under no duty to abide by any of that government's decisions.

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I did not find a statement to that effect, but there was a possibility that there may have been communication between the organ for morale and political information and its superior command that I had -- did not take into consideration. And I believe that the very fact that the superior command has such information at its disposal is tantamount to a signal that this information may also be available to the subordinates in perhaps some other form, not just as a document printed on paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: But that's all speculation, sir.

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could be so. I considered this system to be functioning. This is said from the position of an expert, but you could actually call that speculation although I have no intention to speculate at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Well let's get back to facts. Were you aware that Goran Hadzic of the so-called government arrived on November 20th accompanied by Arkan?

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Not accompanied by Arkan. So this may be a contentious issue whether he was accompanied by Arkan. I know what it means in military terms to be accompanied or escorted by somebody, but they did happen to be there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Were you aware that there is uncontested testimony in this case that Arkan was part of the government delegation that visited Vukovar on November 20th?

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not aware that he was part of the delegation and that it was a delegation at all. But he made public appearances where he was close to the government, so this piece of information does not seem to be very specific because there were such contacts between him and the government in that area. But this did not make me focus my attention on that at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, are you aware that there's uncontested testimony in this case that Arkan would have been arrested in Vukovar had he not been part of that government delegation? Are you aware of that testimony on page 14376?

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not aware of it in this manner that you just put it to me. I was not aware that he was part of the delegation. But he was there with those people, that's clear. But I don't have a clear picture of the arrest situation. I don't know specifically that that was the case. But if this information exists -- this is not something that I can comment, in other words, that he was part of the government. I didn't know that he was part of the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And, sir, as a person who's been involved in security for many years, you know exactly who Arkan is, and you're familiar with his crimes of murder, and torture, and looting, and all of his other crimes.

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to be a bit more specific here. I am aware that there were two versions, two views of Arkan. I wrote an account of one of those versions that I encountered when I was in the field when I retired. Other versions were merely in the public domain, or they were in the domain of rumours. But the version that I was able to put together, I wrote down in an official record, as a retired officer, and I sent it to the security administration for their action.
