So I do have an idea of how Arkan was seen in various contexts by various people who saw him in different ways.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Are you aware that one of the Sljivancanin Defence witnesses testified to his conversation with Arkan prior to the Velepromet meeting - and that's at page 14738 - where he told Arkan that: "You can't start killing or expelling people here, because Tudjman will respond five-fold." Are you familiar with that testimony, sir?

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner, I am not aware of that testimony. I really am not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: May the witness please be shown Exhibit 718, which is 0340-4864 to 4865. For the Court, it's tab 22 in your notebooks.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not all that legible, but please, ask your question and then I will be able to see if I can actually find it in here.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Could you tell me: Who is Mile Babic, Major General Mile Babic, who signed this letter?

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Major General Mile Babic was the chief of the security organ in the 1st Military District.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And in this letter, if you look at the first page, the date is hard to read, but if you are looking at the content?

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: "In a conversation with a OB source, we were given information indicating that Raznjatovic, aka Arkan, and the special police in Dalj commanded by Stricevic Milorad are committing unauthorised killings of arrested ZNG members, arresting Croatian individuals and committing certain acts against the same." The date of this is October 18, 1991. And would you agree that this document talks about allegations of very serious offences against prisoners, the murder of prisoners, and it involves Arkan?

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have to read it through; and then after that, I can answer your question if I can find it in the text the way I understand it. But-- it is a little bit of a problem, but I will try. I've read the first part. I don't know whether we could perhaps scroll down a little bit so I could read the rest of it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: It might be easier if you read it --

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've read it. It's fine. I think I can actually handle it this way, and it's really going fine. So can I now have your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: First, are you familiar with the letter? Have you ever seen this letter before or document previously?

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I have not seen this document before.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you would agree that it concerns the killing or murder of prisoners by Arkan and his special police?

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is what it concerns.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And can you look at the last paragraph of the letter, if you read that. I'll read it: "According to the source, after the organs of the new government had been established in Dalj, various cases, a large number of arrested people were killed and their dead bodies were thrown into the Danube. Some of these --" "... A large number of arrested people were killed and their dead bodies were thrown into the Danube. Some of these bodies turn up," and the next word is illegible, "near the park in Dalj on a daily basis."

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I heard you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: That document from the 1st Military District indicates that there is a serious problem in the protection of prisoners in the new government and in the special police or the so-called special police of Arkan.

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to this document, there is a problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And would you agree, sir, that any government delegation that includes the murderer and criminal Arkan is one that you would be concerned with and probably would not trust?

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: If one had this information when one made one's assessment of this government, one could probably ask one's self whether it is possible to trust this government. But I did not have this document and this is the first time that I see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I would like to correct the transcript which I think might affect the line of questioning of my colleague. On page 48, line 3, when my learned colleague quoted from the text, page 2 of this document, it is -- he read out that the organs of the new government had been established and the actual text is not the new government but the new authorities, and the word "government" is not really used here in this text. On page 1, special police is mentioned under the command of Stricevic Milorad and not by Arkan. So just to make things clear and to have everything correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: If the witness could read on the second page the last paragraph, four lines from the end on the first -- where it says -- the beginning of the last paragraph, [B/C/S spoken]. Could you read it in your language and we'll have the interpreters give the interpretation for confirmation, please.

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: "According to the source, after the establishment of the organs of the new authority, " this is completely illegible now all the way down to the word "process," "a large number of arrested people were killed." So I can't read this part, because it's completely illegible.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your eyesight is better than mine. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well ...

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, would you also agree that based on the reputation of Arkan, that you would be very concerned about handing over any prisoners to any government that includes the murderer Arkan?

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I had information that the government does include this murderer, if I knew that for a fact and if I had the information presented here, I would probably be very, very doubtful of that government.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, when they held this meeting, sir, there's been testimony that the JNA was verbally attacked and insulted. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And there were statements that the locals would not abide by the JNA orders to remove the prisoners to Sremska Mitrovica. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And at the meeting, there were also statements that the locals would prevent the JNA from transporting prisoners to Sremska Mitrovica, if necessary, lying down on the road.

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And would you agree that any government who speaks in this manner insulting and refusing to abide by the JNA orders, which has Arkan in its delegation, is not a government that you'd have a lot of confidence in.

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you allow me, I have to give you any opinion now and what my opinion may have been when I was doing all of this. Now that you add these information to the picture, if I had this information, my conclusions would probably have been different. But I have to say things on the basis of what I had at my disposal at the time when I was writing my expert report as an expert. Because in the events that followed, I actually gave my view of that -- please don't now charge me with forgetfulness, I think it was sometime in September of 1993, off the cuff. I'm trying hard to remember things. But it is quite possible that in the whole huge mass of dates, I may be wrong. But it is very easily possible -- it is very easy to make conclusions on all information that there is. But if you have a civil war, then the conclusions are made on the basis of what can see and what one can achieve at a given time. So I was guided by the fact that I have always been guided by is that one should do everything in an area where I have a mixed population to achieve some kind of justice. It is, of course, hard to apply all of this to everything that happened there. But let me just say that I was born in Croatia and I grew up there. And I am very, very familiar with the relations as they obtained in Croatia. They were part of my assessment that this must be stopped. And the possibility how that might be done is presented in the conclusion. I would probably look at those facts in a much more selective manner had I had this information at my disposal, but it is easy now to say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. I understand, sir. Let's continue on with the government. You would agree that since there were no civilian police, Arkan's special police weren't in Vukovar, that the government needed the local TOs, the local TO to assist in guarding the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: But you also know with regard to the local TO you put in your report, and you've mentioned that General Zivota Panic warned of TO retaliation or revenge -- acts of revenge being taken by local TO units.

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He did warn of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So even though the TO seemed to be the only group available at the time, you knew that there was still a danger involving the TO?

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: In a situation that prevailed in that area and in the wider context, there always was a risk. No solution was risk-free. The question is what was the level of the risk and how one could assess the risk.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: As part of your work in compiling your report, did you see the document or the letter or the report of Petar Stojic in relation to Cyrus Vance's visit to Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weiner, I did have a look at that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you know within Cyrus Vance's report on -- it's page 3 in the B/C/S and page 2 in the English. It's tab 24, page 3 in the B/C/S, page 2 in the English. This concerns Cyrus Vance's November 19th visit to Vukovar. And if you look down page 3, the third paragraph, and in the English on page 2, the four notes up from the bottom, there are four notes of the different notices that Cyrus Vance gave to Mr. Stojic. The second one, "That the members of volunteer and territorial units are behaving in a manner somewhat unfit for a soldier, and they should be put under control as soon as possible."

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see this.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So this was Cyrus Vance's view or report or statement to Mr. Stojic one day prior to the evacuation.

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And not only do we have the November 18th letter from Zivota Panic where it warns of retaliation by the TOs, Cyrus Vance is complaining about unprofessional conduct by the Vukovar TOs and that they should -- and volunteers and that they should be put under control as soon as possible; correct?

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I provide a brief comment on this?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Certainly, sir.

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: You may have noticed that I incorporated this situation in my report. I pointed out the drop in morale and discipline after Vukovar. Some people had started celebrating because they thought that the task had been accomplished. This brought a lot of trouble in terms of military discipline and order, not only trouble for the Territorial Defence, a looser kind of formation than the JNA, but also in the JNA itself. They thought the mission had been completed and they were now allowed more freedom. That's what they thought. And that is why the image that Mr. Vance found when he came there reflected that very moment. However, there is the distinction between unsoldierly appearance and unsoldierly actions that may have been taken, and it seems to be a proven fact. There is a huge distinction, and this is not only about someone's outward unsoldierly appearance. That was the problem for me. So when I talk about that, the question that must be asked is the risky unknowns that occur in every civil war. And in Vukovar, not everything was apparent at first sight, but once the whole thing quietened down, it could have perhaps again made to be tolerable. I'm sorry for taking so long, but this is the essence of my view on this. And the rest may largely be a matter for debate.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: All right, sir. So we have Zivota Panic letter of the 18th. We have Cyrus Vance's letter of unsoldierly like behaviour. Let's look at Exhibit 341, please, which is 0009-9998 through 9999, tab 5. And on tab 5, B/C/S page 2, and the English page 1. On page 1 it's at the bottom under comments, then it says 11.20 comments. In the B/C/S, page 2 it says comments, then it's 11.19 and then 11.20, and then the section on JNA. And this is the second evacuation, not the earlier one where the prisoners were evacuated. This is the evacuation of the sick and wounded. If we look, there's seven points: "No security; many Chetniks; too many officers; only few soldiers; no control; no organising; only a few soldiers to help carry wounded; some Chetniks beat the wounded, shooting in the air, fun; mortar firing from the city." From this, sir -- first, are you familiar with this document?

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you knew, also based on that document, on the 20th that there were problems with volunteers and TO members?

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: In September 1993, I already knew that there had been problems, at least as far as I remember. So it's part of what I was saying. But if you have a situation like that where there is a very sudden transition from a very difficult situation, to a new and unexpected situation, aspects like these are part and parcel of what normally happens. I do apologise, but I do need to go back again. Maybe my own life has contributed to me understanding things the way I understand them, and I only have my own mind to use for thinking. When you have individuals in groups, it's very difficult to exercise any full control over them in situations like these. I did know that things like these had happened, but I also knew that what needed doing was within reach. It was right there for them, and that's why I said that I understood these things to be part of the general euphoria that prevailed. And some people who did what they did got out of hand quite literally. Any civil war is a difficult war. A lot has been written about that, especially in conditions of urban war fare. This incident shows that something got out of hand, got out of control. I observed that, but it certainly was not the rule, rather the exception. That, at least, was my reading of the situation. My view certainly seems to be different.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So, sir, would you agree with Zivota Panic's letter of November 18th that you were to keep -- that the TO and volunteer units must be kept under JNA control to ensure discipline?

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, on the 20th at the barracks, you are aware that they had problems there, that TO members tried to get to the bus -- get to the people on the buses; and that when some 20 to 24 were removed from those buses, that some of them were attacked and beaten. Were you aware of that, sir?

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't aware of the 20 to 24 persons. I didn't have that or, perhaps, it just escaped my attention, but I was aware of the security-related problems. It's something I read about in the documents; that they were aggressive, that they made for the buses. I did address that in my report, and I qualified that in appropriate terms, I think. That's precisely what I tried to address when speaking about the standards that applied in the barracks. There were the standards and there was behaviour deviating from those standards. That was my position and I think I expressed it with sufficient clarity in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And, sir, were you also aware that there were problems at Velepromet, Velepromet holding facility where prisoners were guarded by the local TO and military police? Were you aware of that, sir?

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know exactly about the problems and the extent of any problems, but that there were problems and disagreements about things that some people did. Yes, that's true. There were problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Were you aware that a JNA officer testified that he learned of murders having occurred there? On November 19th, he learned of this?

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm trying to rummage through my recollection to see what remains of all the things that I read and find out at the time. I'm trying to track down this particular bit of information. . But I must tell you the way you put it, I'm not sure I have ever come across anything like that. But I read about problems being encountered and trying to take charge or take control of certain persons over whom no control was meant to be taken.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The interpreter is not entirely sure that he understood the last portion of the witness's answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, the interpreters couldn't fully understand your answer. Could you repeat it, please.

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fine. That's all right. I will. I knew that there were problems about that. I knew that some people, with no regard to their actual powers or remit, were trying to take charge of certain people, exercise control over certain people and, therefore, clashed with the JNA. As for the latter part of your suggestion, I didn't have anything to indicate that there were more serious things happening than the clashes within Velepromet. I hope that now it's more comprehensible.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, so you weren't then aware of the testimony that they had a room at Velepromet known as "the room of death."

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: This sobriquet, this the room of death is not something that I could explain to myself in this sense of people being killed there. My interpretation was that there were people there who were off limits, so to speak, who couldn't be kept outside in the open, so to speak, and within reach of other people. So that, to me, spelled isolation. That's how I understood this sobriquet. But there are several different ways to interpret that. That was my interpretation, but I didn't exactly manage to read the meaning of this room of death.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Well, were you aware that there's been testimony here from civilian witnesses that people were taken out from that room and beaten or disappeared and never -- were never seen again after they left the room of death? Were you aware of that, sir?

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't take that into account. Velepromet was outside the area covered in my expert report in terms of the security function. This was a civilian facility in a neighbourhood in Vukovar where there had been fighting going on. So it might have been somewhat safer, but I wasn't familiar with that evidence; and if I had been familiar with that particular piece of evidence, I probably would have been better able to draw more conclusions and to know more about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: One more mention of that. Were you aware that there was testimony from Colonel Vujic that he notified Colonel Mrksic and Major Sljivancanin of murders at Velepromet on November 20th -- or, actually, Mrksic in the late evening of November 19th, and Sljivancanin on the early morning hours of November 20th, of the murders at Velepromet.

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Vujic? Colonel Vujic saying that, you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes. Were you aware of that testimony?

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must say that I was not aware of that testimony. Not like that. Not that very portion.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Will you agree, sir, based on the exhibits and based on the testimony that -- some of them you hadn't seen until just recently or heard until recently, would you agree that based on that, on what happened on the 18th, 19th and 20th of November, that it was dangerous to place the prisoners under the guard of the Vukovar TO after having seen what they did downtown, what they did at the barracks, and the allegations of murders and beatings at Velepromet?

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now we are talking about this, and we have all the facts assembled in one place. We have all the knowledge resulting from those facts, stemming from those facts. So now certainly, yes, I would tend to agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And, sir, you also are aware, having read a portion of Chief of Staff Danilovic's report, that the hangars at Ovcara were not a safe place for the prisoners either. That portion I read a while ago in the earlier session when we talked about the barracks not being safe?

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. In the first part of my answer to that question, I said this, roughly speaking: Virtually throughout the Vukovar area, there was no really safe place at all. The question was which is safer and which is less safe? But you have to make an on-the-spot assessment, and I can hardly put myself in those shoes and answer that question. I do agree that there was hardly a truly safe place anywhere in the Vukovar area or any places that were safer than others in relative terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, there is uncontested testimony from both JNA and civilian witnesses that in the early afternoon of November 20th when the buses arrived at Ovcara, local TO members and others formed a gauntlet. And that the prisoners had to run through that gauntlet and were beaten with fists, feet, and objects, sticks and metal bars. Were you aware of that testimony?

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was, about the gauntlet. And regarding the overall situation in the barracks, that is consistent and dramatic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And based on this testimony, would you agree with Colonel Panic that there was a serious danger to the prisoners at Ovcara at that time?

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would agree with Colonel Panic regarding the danger to the prisoners, but I would not agree with the way he reacted to that danger.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Well, would you agree that action should have been taken to protect the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most certainly so, especially considering the fact that all those who were meant to be taking measures were all there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And would you also agree with Colonel Panic's statement, it's paragraph 93 in his report -- in his statement to the Office of the Prosecutor, that Colonel Mrksic -- page 25 in the B/C/S -- actually, it begins on 24, tab 26, paragraph 93.

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a minute, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. The expert is being shown witness statements that are not part of evidence here. There is a witness who gave a testimony, and I think in this way, material is being inserted into the expert report that is not part of evidence in this trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. -- Excuse me -- Mr. Weiner, you seem to be putting a statement of somebody to the witness to read. It's not testimony of that witness. Now what is your basis for doing this?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: It was easier to do it where you could read it in front of him, rather than me reading the testimony from trial. The testimony appears on pages 14473 to 14474. This way he can read it in his language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The difficulty, Mr. Weiner, is the possibility that the evidence of the witness is not in accordance with the statement. I haven't sought to compare them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I can just as easily read it from the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think that would be more reliable.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: That's fine, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'm going to read from the transcript. "On November 20th, 1991," this is page 14473, line 23 down. "On the 20th of November, 1991, Colonel Mrksic had all the information necessary to make appropriate decisions to ensure the safety of prisoners from the Vukovar Hospital. There were no interruptions of the system of command," The next page 14474, "... in the system of control command and control or the reporting system that could have prevented him from receiving the most recent information that day. Considering my feelings about the local Serbian TO, and the fact that Colonel Mrksic knew about the threat to the safety of the prisoners posed by the local TO, he could have used units of the Guards Motorised Brigade to neutralise or eliminate this threat. The local Serbian TO was no match for the Guards Motorised Brigade." The witness said, "yes." "Is that what you said?" "Yes." "Q. So according to your statement, you advised Colonel Mrksic of the threat to the safety of those prisoners, and nothing was done to neutralise or eliminate the in threat; isn't that correct?" "A. I told him and I think he reacted. I think he did send some people to Ovcara, but I cannot be certain about it and I don't know any details." Sir, would you agree with that testimony that there was a serious threat, that Mrksic could have sent the Guards Motorised Brigade to neutralise or eliminate that threat?

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: The threat addressed by Lieutenant-Colonel Panic in his evidence means that he was aware of that same threat when he was Chief of Staff of the operations group at Ovcara himself, which means that he should have been better able to see all of it, and to see more, perhaps, than those who came after him to assess the situation. So it's not a communication problem. It's an intervention problem. That is the answer that an expert can give you. Everything else outside that decision is outside my field as an expert. The fact really is what Panic says as a witness, but he is personally involved. He is one of the players in that situation, and I can hardly be expected to say more than I'm saying at the time because then we would have to have a whole new analysis. I'm sorry if I'm not quite hitting the nail on the head or not answering some part of your question. Because if you explain what more you expect me to answer, I will be more than happy to provide any further answers that I can, perhaps, provide.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay, sir. Your Honour, two more areas to cover. Would you like to take the break now, or should I start the next to last area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will take the break now. We will resume at a quarter to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Let's try and finish up today in the next half-hour, 45 minutes. On page 63 in the English, paragraph 13.2, which is below footnote 128, you indicate that the Vukovar TO was subordinated to OG South during part of the day of November 20th. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, on the next page at 64 in the English at 13.4, you indicate that the TO was removed from OG South and then became under the command of the SAO SWBS government; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it says this here.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you must agree, sir, that there are no writings or documents stating that the Vukovar TO was removed from OG South and was now under the command of the SAO SWBS government; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: This can be concluded from what is written here in this text. The text is written in such a way that -- indicating that there were no written documents, but that the approval meant that this task could be carried out only if the TO were to no longer be subordinate to OG South for the period of time that the government needed it. The report states that, although in slightly different terms, so that it's an issue of language and style, that there were no documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, you do indicate on page 67 of the English, section D, that there was, in fact, an order which is provided in the Guards Motorised Brigade OG South war diary at 2.00 in the morning on November 21st. And that is the order to resubordinate the TO.

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, you didn't mention it in your report. But were you aware that four hours later at 6.00 in the morning of November 21st, there is an order from OG South to resubordinate the Vuka TO and Leva Supoderica units? It's tab 13 in your book. It's Exhibit 422. Were you aware of that, sir?

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was aware of that and this did not contradict the first part of the statements that we read about it no longer being part of the OG South, and I can give you an explanation if you want.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Well, if you look at it, first, before you give the explanation, it says: "Vukovar TO units to be resubordinated to the 80th Motorised Brigade and will continue with carrying out the assigned tasks: The provision of security, the patrol of captured areas in Vukovar with an emphasis on the most sensitive facilities: Municipality, post office, SUP, educational and cultural facilities." This document makes clear that the Vukovar TO unit was resubordinated from OG South to the 80th Motorised Brigade?

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. In fact, now you're asking me to give the explanation that could have followed the first one, but this is all about the time line of events and the participants in those events. So now we have to follow this very closely and carefully to see how I was able to reach my conclusions. "First of all, the conclusion was that the government has no other units, apart from the Territorial Defence. Next, if this unit carries out its task, even if it's for just one hour under the jurisdiction of the government because it is a territory-based unit in Vukovar that is under the jurisdiction of the authorities." I am now not going into what this government or authorities were like but just what the regulations were. "In the period while it is performing the tasks outside of OG South for the purposes of the government, regardless of whether there is a written order to that effect, de facto, this time period is the time period during which the unit is not under the control of OG South but under the control of the authorities." "Once this task is completed, the command may issue a document or, rather, pursuant to the same document, the command can still dispose of this unit as it sees fit, because there was no document issued contrary to that." So this is the time line of the events. Written like this, it doesn't look like that because you have one part of the events that are recorded in documents and another part that actually took place in real life and, hence, this discrepancy that appears here in my expert report.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, your conclusion here is little more than speculation because there are no documents supporting what you say. There's no writings and, in fact, the writings all indicate that the Territorial Defence unit was subordinated to OG South, and then they resubordinated the unit on the 20th, the 21st and the 22nd, which is what all the documents state. I'm sorry, the 21st and the 22nd.

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then our interpretations are different. I spoke about the time lines comparing it to the documents. So the interpretation was about how things came about. I was not trying to speculate. I was merely trying to follow the time line of the events, which indicates that the documents -- that the events followed each other in this way. Anybody can understand it the way one wants. But in order to see how the Territorial Defence actually functioned in light of its position, this time line of the events corresponds to the circumstances as they prevailed. I cannot now go into judging those circumstances, whether they were good or bad, because this is not up to me, of course. The picture that you may have may differ from this one. But the way this functioned, I think it was in line about the actual capabilities that existed there. So this is my interpretation and it does not go beyond this.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, but you must admit: Earlier today you've testified that you were going to testify about doctrine, rules and regulations. Now you're testifying not upon doctrine but upon facts as you see them.

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is based on the doctrine because the doctrine made it possible for these things to happen. The doctrine provided for two different elements that functioned separately on different levels, but together as part of the -- as part of the armed forces, the JNA, and the Territorial Defence. And the TO would be brought closer to the JNA when necessary. So you can see the doctrine at work right here. The only thing is this was not expressed in the written form.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you know, sir, knowing rules and regulations, to resubordinate a unit, you have to have a writing.

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a rule, this has to be done in writing, and the resubordination was done in writing. The only thing that was not done in writing was the performance of the -- of an ad hoc task that was not done in writing, but the state of facts could be seen from the actual state of affairs, what happened there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: But you must admit all that the writings indicate that the Territorial Defence unit were subordinated to the JNA on the 20th, the 21st, and the 22nd.

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner, the easiest thing for an expert to do is to read a document, but he needs to know the doctrine and to know what was actually going on. I really tried to understand the doctrine here. I had studied it before. It doesn't follow that the events really conform to the doctrine very closely, but that is one way of looking at things.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Because you know that -- you understand that from the 21st on, every document relating to resubordination, which you don't seem to mention any of them in your report, all indicate the Territorial Defence unit was part of OG South and then the 80th Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not deal with the command and control, until the point when I realised that an interpretation needed to be given that could be understood from the point of view of the doctrine in light of the fact that there was no full explanation. That is why I focused my attention to a certain degree to that. But the answer needed to be given to the question why was there this second document on the resubordination. Because if there had been, if it had been part of the OG South, then there would have been no need for this document. It was obvious that the TO had been removed from OG South and then had to be brought back. On the basis of this, I concluded that the Territorial Defence is now being brought back as part of some kind of resubordination. So there is a gap there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, can you identify what second document are you referring to? Because I didn't see any second document referred to in your report. You said the second document, "why there was there is this second document on the resubordination, if it had been part of OG South." Maybe it's just a translation issue.

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible. I wanted to say that the previous documents, the combat orders, state that the local TO was active as part of OG South. This meant that it was subordinate or resubordinated to the command of the OG South. As such, until this task, it was under the command of OG South, the task that I described here and that I determined to be the point when, in the actual fact, the TO left OG South. Then there was this second order that restored the state of facts to the status quo ante. I think that we misunderstand each other, because the doctrine has to be interpreted very carefully and that is probably one of the problems that we have. That is the only explanation that I have; perhaps, I'm not really very good at conveying it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, you said on page 68, line 13: "Then there was this second order that restored the state of facts to the status quo ante." Sir, we haven't seen any second order restoring the state of facts, as you would say, in this case. Do you have some document that hasn't been used as an exhibit in this case that you are referring to? Because we've never seen any such document here.

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot really find my way because there seemed to be some differences in the way you quote the page references than I do so. Can we now maybe first determine where the quote is, and then we can go on to the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'm reading from your testimony, page 68, line 13: "Then there was this second order that restored the state of facts to the status quo ante." Where is this second order and what is this second order, because we've never seen it here in this courtroom. In fact, sir, if I could -- once you start what's known is if you want to call it the resubordination section, the only order you refer to is on page 67. And it's not an order, it's the order which is referred to in the war diary. There's no other references to any document or any war diary or anything in relation to resubordination of the TO. There aren't any references in your report. So I'm just wondering what is this second order that you've used as a source, because it's not an exhibit in this case.

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now there seems to be a slightly bigger misunderstanding. In the first part, I said that when it comes to the TO, this is it: The initial state was that the Territorial Defence was part of Operations Group South. This can be seen not from the order, but from the combat documents engaging it. As such, these documents are sufficient to make one understand that they -- that it was part of OG South. This was the factual state and that can be seen from the documents. Then, I said that while it was performing tasks for the government that, in practical terms, it no longer was part of OG South for the duration of the performance of the task; and then there was the second order that we just went through together resubordinating the Territorial Defence as stated in the document. This is the time line that I tried to explain. Now, whether there were any other shifts here in the events or terminology, I cannot really clarify that because I don't have everything at my disposal. But this is the gist of what I said. This is what I said. This is what I meant, but probably the context was not complete.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: But, sir, you must agree as you stated: You can't resubordinate a unit without paper, and there was no writings that indicated that that unit was removed from the command of OG South and placed under the command of the government. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be so if these were the organic parts, elements of the JNA units, but the TO, in establishment terms, was not an organic element of the JNA. So when you have a doctrine that divided the JNA from the TO and made both of them independent formations - General Kadijevic spoke about that in his book, his view of the breakdown - there are some differences of opinion here, but we can, in fact, have a debate whether a written document should follow when the TO is subordinated or resubordinated. But I am now talking from the position of an expert in these matters regarding the JNA and the TO and their relationship.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: But sir, your expertise, as you've stated earlier, as is to security organs, it's not to command and control and resubordination; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: This part actually butted into the sphere of security in an indirect way; and as a consequence, I had to deal with it in my report. If necessary, we can actually remove it from the expert report. But I do believe that it provided some further clarifications for the security issues discussed in the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, yesterday, you were asked a question by Mr. Domazet about the exchange of prisoners in the 1st Military District's authorisation of exchanges. Do you recall that yesterday?

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember it was signed by General Stojanovic, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And, sir, were you aware that there was an agreement signed between the nation of Croatia or the government of the Republic of Croatia and the JNA on November 6th in relation to the exchange of prisoners?

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware of this agreement or its contents, so I cannot really give you my opinion from where I am now.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: May the witness please be shown 3D05-0161 in the B/C/S. And in the English, 3D05-0163. 3D05-0161, B/C/S. 3D05-0163. Could you move it down a bit. There's an intro paragraph and then it has the agreement. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Do you see where it says "agreement" in the middle?

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you see one, paragraph one, if you can move it down a little. Thank you. "Both sides concur that they will exchange all prisoners or persons deprived of their liberty on the principle of all for all."

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And in the second paragraph, . "The term prisoner shall be held to include all persons deprived of their liberty who are in prisons, detention facilities, or prison camps, regardless of whether criminal or any other proceedings have been initiated against them, indictments issued, or a final judgement or first instant delivered, regardless of the territory in which they are located or the place they were taken prisoner, deprived of freedom, suffered restrictions of movements, or held hostage." If you -- it continues with 13 paragraphs and if you could bring it down to the bottom, it's signed in November. Do you have page 2? Signed on the 6th of November at Zagreb; Lieutenant General Andrija Raseta and Deputy Minister for Defence Ivan Milas. And this document was issued by the Federal Secretary of National Defence information service. Would you agree, sir, that it wasn't the 1st Military District that determined exchanges. Based on this agreement, it was the Federal Secretary of National Defence pursuant to an agreement.

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It is correct that he was the Federal Secretary of National Defence and the signatories of this agreement have been empowered to do so, because Raseta could not have done that without the approval of his superiors. This is the principle of chain of command and the responsibility for what one does. So I agree with you, yes. The 1st Military District did not have all the powers to deal with the prisoners as it saw fit.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to offer that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 869, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'd like to cover one last issue, area, or topic with you. And it concerns page 67 of your report in the English, just after footnote 145. It starts -- that's the section known as events after the evacuation of the hospital. That's the section of your -- and if you could turn to paragraph 6 of that section which is on page 68. In the English, it's right at the bottom, the last two lines. It goes into page 69 just above your conclusion. Basically to save -- why don't you take a look at it first. To summarise it, to save some time, it basically says that you couldn't find any documents indicating that the security organ was aware of the massacre at Ovcara, and that it was your conclusion that the massacre was covered up from the security organ. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think -- oh, yes, that's a totally different thing. Now I see your point. The documents indicate that the sources and what should have been the basis for the operation of the security organs were not open enough for the activities to actually start. I have an example for that, but I will not go into that, maybe later on if the need arises. It is stated here that the sources of the security organs were the JNA. If they did not share the information in such a way that it was impossible for the activities to start right away, then there was this problem that the security organs had to deal with short-term or long-term. This was the principle of social self-protection which was a widespread principle that prevailed at that time, and that was the basis that the security organs used to actually be able to operate as security organs. The problems occurred when, at the first stage of social self-protection, there was some resistance or some obstacles put to the inflow of information. And that is why this is put in here both on the basis of the experience, and this is by way of an example, when there couldn't have been a response of any kind. And that's all there is here.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Just very briefly, if the security organ received information that a massacre had occurred, that murders had occurred, what were they supposed to do? What was it their duty to do, as briefly as possible?

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you look at my previous answer, that suggests what the next step would be if they had information telling them whether to start operative work or not. If the Chamber allows, I might be able to give an explanation to show what sort of difficulty may arise. It's of a purely procedural nature, and it does have a bearing on my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: It's fine. Please.

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I? You showed me the report sent by General Babic to the security administration. This is a typical example of how certain events are not recorded the way they should be. Information was conveyed that was reliable, if indeed it was reliable, which would have had to elicit a reaction from whoever had obtained this particular piece of information. General Babic had Arkan in his own territory that he was responsible for. He writes this document. He sends it off to the security administration without specifying whether he in fact informed his own commander. Now what does that mean? I'm taking us back to square one, where we left off. If the security organ had retrieved reliable information, such information as General Babic had retrieved, they would have had to send their own commander and send a report to their superior command, but there's nothing reliable that I can cross based on which I would have been entitled to say that the security organs had sufficient information available to them to do what they did. So there is your explanation for why the situation was the way it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, you're familiar with the names or some of the personnel who were in the security organ in the Guards Motorised Brigade Operations Group South. You're familiar with some of the people or at least their names?

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must say I became familiar with those names later, but I wasn't earlier on. One of them may have attended the -- one of my lectures. As for any previous meetings, I told you about the previous meetings; Bojinovic there, Sljivancanin here. I'm trying to remember if I can remember anyone else, but I don't think that really matters. But not prior to that, no, I hadn't seen anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, Major Vukasinovic served as the assistant head of staff for security, are you aware of that? And that's probably not the number one, but the number two deputy under Major Sljivancanin.

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I do know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Are you aware that he testified in this court that on the morning of November 21st, he was advised that the people at Ovcara had disappeared and were taken away or murdered. Were you aware of that testimony?

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware of that testimony. But now that you've told me about it, perhaps I could comment. May I? Excellent. If indeed Major Vukasinovic stated that, for me, as a counter-intelligence and security officer, the question would be: How did he use that information? What did he do next? Did he write it down? Did he pass it on to his superior? Did he pass this along followed by advice on what to do next? Because that would be the correct procedure followed by any security officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, were you aware, sir, that Major Vukasinovic's deputy in the security organ of OG South was Mile Bozic? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vukasinovic. I think Vukasinovic could not have had a deputy. He was a desk officer. I don't think there were any deputies there. That's a different thing, assistants, yes, perhaps. I don't know. I didn't study Mile Bozic's position. He didn't seem that important. He was inside a security organ that was run by Veselin Sljivancanin, and I didn't go into those relationships.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, were you aware that there is testimony that Captain Bozic heard about the murders or disappearance on November 21st and advised Major Vukasinovic of that -- of the disappearance of the prisoners? And that's at page 15048 is that testimony.

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't aware of what Bozic had told Vukasinovic, but again, we are back with Vukasinovic, his work and his responsibilities. That's where the matter lies. And we have the same thing now as we did when you previously told me that Vukasinovic had known that he had been informed. Yes, but the question is: What next? Okay. We are with Vukasinovic. I want to see if we can push it further from there, if we can sort of detach ourselves from Vukasinovic and move further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't mean to interrupt this thread, one correction though. When Mr. Vukasinovic testified, Mile Bozic was not described as his deputy in the security organ, but as his deputy in his capacity as the Negoslavci town commander. The question might have been different. He testified about himself being from the military police, so this is a role totally outside the security organ.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'm just reading from the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'm just reading from the transcript: "Your deputy's name?" "Captain Bozic Mile."

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Let's continue, sir. Sir, you must agree, based on this testimony, that at least one member or more of the security organ of the Guards Motorised Brigade, OG South, did become aware on the morning of November 21st of the disappearance of prisoners and possible murder. That it wasn't withheld with them, because one has testified here that he knew about it.

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: One or more is a great deal of difference when speaking about a security organ. The way I see it, Bozic was not a security officer, not a member of the security organ. He was the deputy town commander, deputy to Ljubisa Vukasinovic at Negoslavci, which was a position well outside the security organ. I can't help asking myself, why was Vukasinovic a town commander. But let's leave it for the time being. What's the difference between one person knowing and many people knowing? What's the difference about that? Well, let's discuss that. What if one person knew, what did they do about it? I don't know. What can I say? What I heard, I heard from you. I commented on that. I can hardly be expected to provide an answer to that question, which means he took note of this and that's the way it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, you placed in your statement that the matter was covered up from the security organ. Major Vukasinovic's testimony indicates that he wasn't [as interpreted]. That he was told on the morning of November 21st, 1991. That he was told. It says that he wasn't told.

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I say about knowledge, what the security organs knew, I look at Sljivancanin's position because he's in charge of the security organ. What doesn't get as far as the chief of the security organ in terms of verified information confirmed, if you like, or corroborated, is not something that that part of the organisational part of the security organ deals with, but rather which ever individual receives it. The problem is if this is now done, this is no longer useful for the security organ. I'm talking about useful information, information that can be used, information that can be used to start an activity. This is a passive attitude and allows for no action. Now, for me, as an expert, this is a problem. Are there any aspects, I don't know, I can't answer that. As an expert, I do know that as long as information is not used to start an activity, it must remain closed somewhere. Reserved, if you like.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, you were shown a number of documents. Did anyone ever show you Major Vukasinovic's statement before the military prosecutor in Belgrade? Did anyone ever show you that statement?

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't shown that statement, Mr. Weiner. I wasn't shown that statement and I didn't read it. Therefore, I can say with full responsibility that I have no idea what he said in that statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Because he says: "We found out that all the persons on Ovcara had disappeared during the night and that their destiny was unknown." So no one showed you that statement in relation to Major Vukasinovic?

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody has ever shown me this statement. But it would be interesting if they said for example, we discovered; and then that "we," we can see what the "we" is, who the "we" is, because this is a nameless way of speaking. Naming no names. What does that mean? "We did." "We are." We have to know who discovered or who disclosed what and who took part in that or who was involved. I don't think this would allow me to do what I would truly like to do, to see whether that was started. And this "we." This "we" is what constitutes the problem in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: We've had other testimony in this case. We've had testimony from a Defence witness who was one of the higher members of the Guards Motorised Brigade, who learned of the murders on November 21st and the 22nd as the soldiers and the officers at the command were discussing it. Were you aware of that, sir? That's on page 12442. Were you aware of that testimony, sir?

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. But I'm talking about what was found in the security organs. What circulated without ever reaching the security organs is not something that I, as an expert, can include as one of the things that have to do with the security organ. I think my position, the position that I'm trying to speak about is very clear. I'm talking about information that eventually reached the security organ and that may have been circulated among people but concealed to prevent anybody from knowing about this information. If anybody knew about this, I would have had to find it somewhere in the security organ. That's why my position is what it is, and this position is based on elements that were available to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: But you must accept, sir, that it couldn't have been hidden from the security organ if the number two deputy to Major Sljivancanin knew about it on the morning of November 21st. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: Allow me, sir. Again, I'm supposed to be an expert and not somebody who is on the spot and tries to tell what each individual is doing. I don't have those elements. As an expert, we can sit side-by-side, and you, for example, are never able to find out something that I simply don't want to tell you. It is not to be ruled out that Major Vukasinovic did know about that. But I can't say that he did anything for that to become general knowledge in the security organ forks someone to start something, for someone to do something about it. So that's the real problem for me. I just can't ... Knowledge, you say, of at least one of them knew, well, I accept one of them knew, that may as well be right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honours. I hope that my learned friend has concluded. I believe there is an error on page 79, lines 22 through 23, when my learned friend quoted from what was stated at page 12442 of the transcript. He says that this was stated by one of the higher ranking officers of the Guards Motorised Brigade. When in fact, this is Danilovic, chief of the staff of the 80th Motorised Brigade. So that's the only discrepancy. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may. If I may comment on this, because that directly concerns my answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: It should read 80th Motorised Brigade. It should be.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you a question related to that. The command of the 80th Motorised Brigade and the command of the Guards Motorised Brigade were both located in Negoslavci; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And we know when we're talking about Negoslavci, we're not dealing with a metropolis. We're not talking about London, Tokyo, New York City. We're dealing with a small village; correct?

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And if the officers and soldiers of the 80th are discussing it, there's nothing preventing the officers and soldiers of the Guards Motorised Brigade to be knowing what's going on; wouldn't you agree?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you know, all right, I must look at that relationship in light of what it actually was. There was a very serious duality, and I did state there was this really serious move that indicated that this event was not really something that was much rumoured at the time by persons who were there. No matter of these persons were persons that just happened to get wind of something or actually knew something more about it. From the point of view of security work and responsible and serious behaviour, we don't have a single element indicating that the link-ups and the behaviour was such, in terms of the establishment, in terms of the practicalities and everything else, to indicate that there was that degree of closeness or a close-knit relationship. I've never come across anything like that. You say such knowledge was possible. Maybe it was possible, but this is the sort of event that people would not too easily start talking about unconfirmed, unverified stories. I know that based on my experience, and I know that based on very specific data points. Was that possible? Well that's a problem for us to tackle. In some other way, a third way, a fourth way, or a fifth way for this to spread, I really can't say. The environment is gone. It's gone forever. We can't recreate the original environment. Since I can't recreate the original environment, there is no way I can possibly see if any omissions or mistakes were made or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Please, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think the question was speculative and the answer is now speculative. It's no use to us now. The witness was asked to speculate and that's just as good as the answer was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Carry on, Mr. Weiner. You've heard the force of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, isn't it the job of security organ to go out and find information? Not just to sit and wait for a telephone call from a source. It's their job to go out and seek information. Isn't that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: Petar Vuga [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. That's quite correct. I'm not talking about that. I'm not saying that they did a good job or didn't do a good job or whether, indeed, such information was available at all. That's a different kettle of fish. We might talk about that if you like. It's about evaluating the professional abilities of whoever is involved, but the situation I found is the situation I found. So between what could have been done and between what was eventually done is this: I did not come across anything to indicate that any information that was available was available in such a way as to give rise as to give sufficient reason for anyone to start an action. Was this sort of information available or not? Well, that's a question which remains for me without an answer. Why? Because I never ventured upon a hypothesis like that not knowing the environment or the brigade that left. And now this gives a totally different set of references on my work. So that's a different question and it requires a different answer, and I'm afraid this is an answer which I'm not well able to provide.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Can we go into private session, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you had an objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This question, again, calls for speculation. Mr. Weiner fails to identify, although we were in private session, where these persons might have heard what he thinks they heard. That's in relation to what he was saying about Mr. Vukasinovic. If that's the question, then I think we're well outside the scope of what this witness, as an expert witness, might be able to tell us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The proposition being questioned is an assertion in the report of the experts that information of these matters were being kept from the security organ. So questioning which identified those who had a connection with the security organ who, in their evidence here, have said they know of it or knew of it at the time on the morning of the 21st of November is appropriate. Now, Mr. Weiner, it's got a little trouble, but I'm sure Mr. Lukic has some re-examination. That being so, we must adjourn for the day to continue tomorrow at 9.00. And in view of that confusion, if you find in the morning that you haven't quite finished, we would allow you to continue just a little more. Otherwise, we treat you as having finished your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: He didn't answer the last question, so I'm not finished until the answer, Your Honour okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We adjourn until tomorrow resuming at 9.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 7th day of December, 2006, at 9.00 a.m. 17 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
